entry.title: Rethinking Zero-Knowledge TLS: Proof of Protocol Execution and the Reclaim Protocol
entry.summary:
In a zkTLS protocol, a user proves to a third party a property of data obtained from an online service over TLS, revealing nothing beyond the statement proven. Each existing scheme, however, comes with its own security model, written for that scheme alone, so the schemes are not proven secure against a common definition. The root cause is a mismatch of levels: existing models are stated at the level of TLS and therefore reflect how each construction handles it.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #rust #distributed-systems

entry.title: On the Security of MPC-in-the-Head Signatures with Correlated GGM Trees
entry.summary:
Recent MPC-in-the-Head techniques enable the construction of signature schemes with compact signature sizes from various hardness assumptions. These techniques rely on commitments based on GGM trees, which have been optimized to further reduce the signature size with the so-called one-tree or correlated tree optimizations. While the one-tree technique has no incidence on the security of the scheme, this is not obvious for the correlated tree technique, and a formal security analysis of this technique has been missing in the literature.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #post-quantum

entry.title: Phoenix: Hash-and-Sign with Aborts from Lattice Gadgets
entry.summary:
Preimage sampling is a fundamental tool in lattice-based cryptography, and its performance directly impacts that of the cryptographic mechanisms relying on it. In 2012, Micciancio and Peikert proposed a new way of generating trapdoors (and an associated preimage sampling procedure) with very interesting features. Unfortunately, in some applications such as digital signatures, the performance may not be as competitive as other approaches like Fiat-Shamir with Aborts.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #post-quantum #combinatorics

entry.title: Ideal Pseudorandom Code, Revisited
entry.summary:
Pseudorandom error-correcting codes (PRCs), introduced by Christ and Gunn at CRYPTO’24, combine pseudorandomness with error correction, providing a natural abstraction for robust watermarking and steganography on generative AI models. Subsequent standalone notions, which are ideal security for secret-key PRCs and CCA-style security for public-key PRCs, are oracle-based and do not capture composable use with explicit parties, sessions, and corruption. We give a UC treatment of PRCs via corruption-aware ideal functionalities for both settings.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #compilers #combinatorics

entry.title: Aker: Efficient Two-Party SLH-DSA
entry.summary:
Threshold signing is widely deployed to protect cryptographic keys, but extending these deployments to post-quantum signatures remains challenging. While NIST's lattice-based signatures now have efficient threshold protocols, distributed signing for SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), NIST's stateless hash-based signature standard, has been considered prohibitively expensive because it lacks the algebraic structure those protocols typically exploit. We present Aker, a maliciously secure two-party signing protocol compatible with an unmodified FIPS 205 verifier.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #distributed-systems #post-quantum

entry.title: Sunshine Systems: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Compliance with Freedom of Information Laws
entry.summary:
Freedom of information laws (informally known as Sunshine Laws), such as the US Federal Freedom of Information Act, provide legal pathways for members of the public to compel governments to produce internal documentation. These laws have become a powerful tool for government accountability, allowing journalists and activists to uncover malfeasance and advocate for change. However, because compliance with these laws requires government actors---the same entities who may be accused of malfeasance---to produce documentation, there is a risk that evidence of malfeasance may be suppressed rather than produced in response to a query.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #combinatorics

entry.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
entry.summary:
We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup. QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement.

Source: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive · Tags: #cryptography #zkp #rust #consensus
